entries.name: Tirzepatide Franchise (Mounjaro / Zepbound)
entries.thesisShort: Eli Lilly's tirzepatide franchise generated $14.87 billion in Q2 2026 alone — nearly two-thirds of company revenue — while the oral follow-up Foundayo (orforglipron) launched to a soft $98 million start.
entries.thesisLong:
Eli Lilly's tirzepatide is the highest-grossing pharmaceutical franchise in the world, and the gap to Novo Nordisk has widened rather than closed.

Q2 2026 worldwide revenue was $23.0 billion, up 48% year over year. Mounjaro, the type 2 diabetes presentation, grew 91% to $9.94 billion; Zepbound, the obesity presentation, grew 46% to $4.93 billion. Together they accounted for almost two-thirds of total company revenue. Across the first half of 2026 tirzepatide brought in roughly $27.7 billion, putting Lilly more than $10.2 billion ahead of Novo Nordisk on incretin revenue against a gap of under $2 billion a year earlier. Lilly raised its 2026 outlook again alongside the print.

The oral chapter has begun, and it started slowly. Foundayo — orforglipron, Lilly's oral GLP-1 — generated $98 million in the quarter, described by the company as very early in launch but visibly lagging Novo's oral Wegovy, which did $497 million over the same period. That is the single most important development for anyone underwriting Lilly's next leg: the injectable franchise is compounding, but the pill that was supposed to open the mass-market, supply-unconstrained channel is behind its direct competitor out of the gate.

The manufacturing thesis remains the structural moat. Lilly has committed tens of billions to US API and fill-finish capacity precisely because incretin supply, not demand, has governed revenue for three years, and the company that can physically make more doses captures the market.

Risks are policy and competition: IRA price negotiation eventually reaching tirzepatide, next-generation entrants including Viking's VK2735 and Amgen's MariTide, and any adverse signal in long-duration outcomes data.

entries.name: Semaglutide Franchise (Ozempic / Wegovy)
entries.thesisShort: Novo Nordisk's injectable franchise has flattened — Ozempic grew 3% and injectable Wegovy 1% in Q2 2026 — but the Wegovy pill has launched strongly at $497 million in its quarter.
entries.thesisLong:
Novo Nordisk built the obesity market and is now defending it against a competitor with a larger franchise and faster growth. The Q2 2026 numbers make the shape of that defence clear.

Injectable growth has essentially stopped. Ozempic recorded worldwide sales of about $4.8 billion, up 3% year over year, and injectable Wegovy $3.0 billion, up 1%. Against Lilly's Mounjaro at +91% and Zepbound at +46% in the same quarter, that is not a share fight Novo is winning on the injectable side.

The oral franchise is where Novo is ahead. The Wegovy pill generated $497 million in Q2 2026, roughly five times what Lilly's competing Foundayo managed in the same period. Novo got the oral formulation to market and to scale first, and the pill is the format that reaches patients who refuse injections and channels that cannot handle cold-chain pens — a genuinely different addressable population rather than a substitution of its own injectable base.

The supply chokepoint that defined 2023-2024 is now largely internalised. Novo Holdings' acquisition of Catalent moved three fill-finish sites inside the group, which is why fill-finish capacity no longer gates Wegovy the way it once did — and why the merchant CDMO market lost a large block of capacity to a single buyer.

The risks now run through pricing and pipeline rather than manufacturing: US price concessions compressing gross margin, continued tirzepatide share gains, and the need for next-generation assets to re-establish growth on the injectable side.

entries.name: VK2735 Dual GLP-1/GIP Agonist
entries.thesisShort: Viking is the most credible third entrant in the incretin race, with both Phase 3 VANQUISH trials fully enrolled and the oral VK2735 Phase 3 now slated to start in Q4 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
Viking Therapeutics is the most credible independent third entrant in the incretin race, and 2026 has been an enrolment year rather than a data year.

The subcutaneous Phase 3 obesity programme comprises VANQUISH-1 and VANQUISH-2. VANQUISH-1 completed enrolment in November 2025; VANQUISH-2, which enrolled approximately 1,000 patients, completed enrolment in March 2026. VANQUISH-2 is a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial of once-weekly subcutaneous VK2735 over 78 weeks, with percent change in body weight as the primary endpoint and thresholds at 5%, 10%, 15% and 20% weight reduction as secondary measures. A 78-week endpoint on a study that finished enrolling in March 2026 puts topline data well into 2027 — the timeline is the single most important fact for anyone modelling this name.

The oral programme has slipped. Initiation of the Phase 3 oral VK2735 obesity trial is now expected in Q4 2026, later than the Q3 2026 previously indicated. That matters more than a one-quarter delay normally would, because both Novo and Lilly have already launched oral incretins commercially — Viking's oral asset is now entering Phase 3 into a market with two approved competitors rather than an open field.

The structural exposure is unchanged and severe: this is effectively a single-asset company whose value turns on two readouts, with no commercial-scale manufacturing of its own and a capital requirement that grows as the programmes advance.

entries.name: Sterile Fill-Finish Capacity
entries.thesisShort: With Catalent taken private by Novo Holdings, Thermo Fisher's Patheon network is the largest listed independent representative of the sterile fill-finish chokepoint — six facilities supporting aseptic manufacturing worldwide.
entries.thesisLong:
Sterile fill-finish is the step where a biologic becomes a dose: filling vials, cartridges and pen devices under aseptic conditions. It is capital-intensive, heavily regulated, slow to qualify, and it is where injectable supply is physically rationed.

The listed representation of this chokepoint narrowed sharply when Novo Holdings acquired Catalent and moved three fill-finish sites in-house to serve Novo's own GLP-1 volumes. That removed the purest public proxy and took a large block of capacity out of the merchant market simultaneously. Thermo Fisher's Patheon network is now the largest listed independent representative: six facilities support aseptic manufacturing and sterile fill-finish globally, including a 24,000 square metre Singapore site with a high-speed, fully automated aseptic line for both small and large molecules.

Thermo Fisher itself is performing. Q2 2026 revenue was $11.99 billion, up 10% including 5% organic growth, with GAAP diluted EPS of $4.68 and adjusted EPS of $6.03, and the company raised its 2026 outlook. Growth was led by the laboratory products and biopharma services business.

The honest limitation of this entry is proportionality. Sterile fill-finish is a modest slice of a diversified $12 billion-per-quarter instruments and services conglomerate, so Thermo Fisher's reported results are a weak read on fill-finish tightness specifically. Anyone using this entry as a fill-finish gauge should treat it as the best available listed proxy rather than a direct one — the pure-play has been taken private, and no equivalent replaced it.

The demand drivers remain intact: GLP-1 pens, injectable biologics, ADCs and biosimilars all need aseptic fill, and the EU Annex 1 revision forces a reinvestment cycle in high-specification capacity.

entries.name: Bioprocessing Consumables & Filtration
entries.thesisShort: Repligen sells the bags, filters and Protein A resins every biologics facility consumes by the kilogram; Q2 2026 organic growth accelerated to 13% with margins up 460 basis points and guidance raised.
entries.thesisLong:
Repligen sells the consumables that biologics manufacturing burns through continuously — single-use bags and assemblies, filtration systems, chromatography hardware and Protein A affinity resins. Every monoclonal antibody, ADC and cell therapy facility buys them repeatedly, which makes this a recurring toll on the entire biologics build-out rather than a capital-equipment cycle.

Q2 2026 showed the bioprocessing recovery accelerating rather than merely continuing. Revenue was $204 million, up 12% as reported and 13% organically, with the CEO noting sequential acceleration and continued market outperformance. Profitability moved faster than revenue: adjusted income from operations reached $34 million against $22 million a year earlier, non-GAAP adjusted EPS was $0.54 versus $0.37, and margins expanded 460 basis points. The company raised full-year organic revenue and EPS guidance.

Margin expansion at that pace in a consumables business is the signal worth isolating, because it indicates volume leverage on installed capacity rather than price — the pattern that appears when customers move from destocking back to normal consumption.

The demand vectors ahead are the ADC manufacturing build-out, which is filtration- and resin-intensive; process intensification driven by very large-volume products; cell and gene therapy commercial launches; and the biosimilar wave reaching the US.

The competitive risk is structural: Sartorius, Cytiva and Thermo Fisher all bundle consumables with equipment and can price the attach aggressively. CDMO destocking cycles and China biopharma exposure under BIOSECURE-type rules are the other exposures.

entries.name: GLP-1 Elastomer & Containment Components
entries.thesisShort: West makes the elastomer stoppers, plungers and seals inside every GLP-1 pen and vial; Q2 2026 revenue rose 13.8% to $872.3 million and the company raised both sales and EPS guidance for 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
West Pharmaceutical Services makes the parts of an injectable drug that are not the drug: the elastomer stoppers, plungers, seals and needle shields that sit inside every vial, cartridge and pen. Each autoinjector uses several of them, and every one must be qualified with the specific molecule it contacts — which is why switching suppliers mid-programme is close to impossible and why this is a genuine chokepoint rather than a commodity supply line.

Q2 2026 beat on both lines. Revenue was $872.3 million, up 13.8% year over year, with adjusted EPS of $2.37, up 28.8%. Management raised full-year 2026 sales guidance to $3.345-3.380 billion from $3.29-3.35 billion and adjusted EPS guidance to $8.85-9.05 from $8.40-8.75 — a raise at both the top and bottom line, with EPS raised proportionally more, which points at high-value product mix rather than volume alone.

Management attributed the quarter to strong demand in biologics, GLP-1 elastomers and high-value product components. High-value products are the margin engine here: the coated and film-laminated components required for sensitive biologics and for compliance with the EU Annex 1 revision, which is forcing a multi-year upgrade cycle across the industry's fill lines.

The structural position holds as long as injectables grow — GLP-1 pens, ADCs, biosimilars and the shift of oncology and immunology therapies into autoinjector formats all expand container-closure demand.

The exposures are customer concentration among the largest GLP-1 makers, destocking risk if those customers over-order, and execution on the capacity expansions being built for Annex 1 compliance.

entries.name: Casgevy Gene Therapy & Rare Disease Franchise
entries.thesisShort: Vertex is the cash-generating engine of commercial gene therapy; Casgevy revenue reached $76 million in Q2 2026, up 151% year over year, and the FDA approved it for children as young as two.
entries.thesisLong:
Vertex is the rare company that funds gene therapy commercialisation out of its own operating cash flow rather than capital markets, using a dominant cystic fibrosis franchise to underwrite Casgevy, acute pain and type 1 diabetes programmes simultaneously.

Q2 2026 total revenue was $3.3 billion, up 12%, and the non-CF products finally became visible. Casgevy generated $76 million in the quarter — up 78% sequentially and 151% year over year — which is the inflection the ramp had been waiting for after a slow start gated by authorised treatment centre capacity and the months-long patient journey each infusion requires. Journavx delivered $50 million against $12 million a year earlier.

The regulatory news is the more durable development. The FDA approved Casgevy in children two years of age and older with sickle cell disease or transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia, making it the first genetic therapy indicated for children as young as two in both conditions. Treating earlier means treating before irreversible organ damage accumulates, which changes both the clinical case and the addressable population.

Vertex raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $13.1-13.2 billion from $12.95-13.1 billion, including expectations of $500 million or more from non-CF products.

The type 1 diabetes programme is in flux: the company is weighing whether to bring the Type O candidate to market first or close behind zimislecel, with updated plans and timelines expected in the second half of 2026 — an unresolved strategic question rather than a scheduled catalyst.

entries.name: In Vivo CRISPR Editing Pipeline
entries.thesisShort: CRISPR Therapeutics owns the platform side of Casgevy plus the deepest in vivo CRISPR pipeline, with CTX340 and CTX460 both now in Phase 1 and a CTX310 durability update due at ESC Congress in August 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
CRISPR Therapeutics is the platform half of Casgevy — Vertex commercialises it — and its more consequential value driver is the in vivo pipeline, where a lipid nanoparticle delivers the editor to the liver rather than requiring cells to be removed, edited and reinfused.

That pipeline moved from preclinical to clinical across 2026. CTX340, targeting angiotensinogen for refractory hypertension, received FDA IND clearance and has entered a Phase 1 trial. CTX460, targeting SERPINA1 for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and the first candidate from the company's SyNTase editing platform, has also entered Phase 1. CTX321, targeting LPA for elevated lipoprotein(a), is in development alongside them, giving three cardiovascular in vivo programmes plus AATD.

CTX310, the ANGPTL3 programme for familial hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemias and severe hypertriglyceridemia, is the most advanced. A late-breaking abstract on the durability of its effects was accepted for the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Munich on 28 August 2026, with a Phase 1b clinical update expected in the second half of the year. Durability is the specific question that determines whether one-time in vivo editing displaces chronic therapy, which makes that presentation the most informative near-term event on the calendar.

The company raised $600 million in convertible notes during the quarter, funding the clinical programmes without depending on Casgevy economics.

The field-level risk is a safety event in any in vivo CRISPR programme, which would affect every developer at once, alongside the known limitation that LNP delivery reaches the liver far more readily than other tissues.

entries.name: Post-Keytruda Oncology Pipeline
entries.thesisShort: Merck's Keytruda grew 5% to $8.37 billion in Q2 2026, and the subcutaneous version — Keytruda Qlex — reached $463 million in its second quarter, tracking toward 30-40% US adoption by the end of 2027.
entries.thesisLong:
Merck's central problem is well known: Keytruda is the world's best-selling drug and its US compound patent protection ends at the end of the decade, so the equity turns on what replaces it.

The most substantive answer so far is reformulation, and it is working faster than expected. Q2 2026 Keytruda sales rose 5% to $8.37 billion, of which $463 million came from Keytruda Qlex, the subcutaneous formulation — up from $128 million in Q1 2026, more than tripling in a single quarter and surpassing investor expectations. Merck reports double-digit Qlex adoption as a share of the total US business and a path to 30-40% adoption by the end of 2027.

The strategic logic is that a subcutaneous injection administered in minutes carries its own intellectual property and a materially different administration economics from a lengthy intravenous infusion. Converting a large share of the franchise before biosimilar intravenous pembrolizumab arrives blunts the erosion, because a biosimilar of the IV product does not automatically substitute for the subcutaneous one. How much of the base converts by 2028-2029 is the single most important variable in this entry.

Company-wide, Q2 2026 worldwide sales were $16.6 billion and Merck raised 2026 revenue guidance to $66.3-67.3 billion from $65.8-67.0 billion, with contributions from newer launches building.

The risks are unchanged in kind: biosimilar entry timing, the need for pipeline assets to carry meaningful revenue by the end of the decade, and IRA price negotiation broadening into oncology.

entries.name: Seagen ADC Portfolio & Oncology Reset
entries.thesisShort: Pfizer's Seagen-derived ADC portfolio is delivering: Padcev grew 23% operationally in Q2 2026 and won FDA approval as the first platinum-free perioperative regimen for muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
entries.thesisLong:
Pfizer paid $43 billion for Seagen to buy an antibody-drug conjugate platform rather than a single product, and 2026 has produced the clearest evidence yet that the assets are moving into larger populations.

Padcev, the enfortumab vedotin ADC marketed with Astellas, posted 23% operational revenue growth in Q2 2026 on expanded share in first-line locally advanced or metastatic urothelial cancer. More importantly, Pfizer and Astellas announced FDA approval of Padcev in combination with pembrolizumab as neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment for adults with muscle-invasive bladder cancer regardless of cisplatin eligibility, based on the Phase 3 EV-304 (KEYNOTE-B15) trial. That is the first platinum-free regimen approved in this setting, and moving an ADC from metastatic into perioperative use is the transition that multiplies treated patients — earlier-line approvals reach far more people than late-line ones.

The wider company is stabilising around the oncology franchise. Non-COVID revenue grew 18% operationally in Q2 2026, Eliquis contributed $2.43 billion on 19% operational growth helped by lower US rebates and favourable channel mix, and Pfizer raised full-year guidance by $500 million at the midpoint to $60.5-62.5 billion.

The risks remain class-level and structural. ADC-class interstitial lung disease scrutiny applies across every developer in the category, and Pfizer still faces loss of exclusivity pressure on older products that the oncology portfolio has to outgrow rather than merely offset.

entries.name: Post-Eliquis / Opdivo Growth Portfolio
entries.thesisShort: Bristol Myers' growth portfolio rose 14% in Q2 2026 and Eliquis grew 22% to $4.48 billion, with full-year Eliquis growth now guided to 20-25% — the anticipated erosion has not yet appeared in reported results.
entries.thesisLong:
Bristol Myers Squibb's thesis has been a race between the decline of two enormous legacy products and the ramp of a growth portfolio meant to replace them. In 2026 the legacy side has held up better than the framing assumed.

Eliquis grew 22% in Q2 2026 to $4,481 million, and full-year 2026 Eliquis revenue growth is now guided to 20-25%. Whatever generic exposure is coming, it has not yet appeared in reported results, and the near-term revenue base is stronger than a straightforward cliff narrative implies. Opdivo is the softer half: first-half 2026 sales of $4.63 billion were down 3.9% year over year, so the immuno-oncology franchise is eroding while the anticoagulant is not.

The growth portfolio rose 14% in the quarter, and Bristol Myers raised both revenue and adjusted EPS guidance for the full year, with Q2 EPS of $1.62.

Cobenfy remains the highest-variance asset. It grew 81% to $63 million — a large percentage on a small base — and the company has flagged slow physician titration to effective doses and repeat prescribing as the practical constraints in schizophrenia. Those are commercial execution problems rather than efficacy problems, but they are the ones that determine whether Cobenfy becomes a major franchise or a modest one, and they will apply again in any Alzheimer's psychosis indication.

The risk shape has therefore shifted: less about an imminent Eliquis cliff, more about whether the growth portfolio compounds fast enough before Opdivo's decline steepens.

entries.name: Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM)
entries.thesisShort: Dexcom grew Q2 2026 revenue 13% to $1.308 billion with gross margin up 400 basis points on the G7 15-day transition, and won the first FDA clearance for an over-the-counter CGM in children.
entries.thesisLong:
Dexcom is the reference continuous glucose monitor in the United States, and 2026 has been a year of margin structure improving alongside addressable population expanding.

Q2 2026 revenue was $1.308 billion, up 13% reported and 12% organically, with US revenue up 11% and international up 19% reported. The more consequential line is gross margin at 64.1%, up 400 basis points year over year, driven by manufacturing efficiencies and the transition to the G7 15-day system. Extending sensor wear from ten to fifteen days cuts the number of sensors a patient consumes per year, which lowers Dexcom's cost to serve while improving the patient experience — the rare change that helps both sides. The company is on track to convert roughly 50% of its US customer base to extended wear by the end of 2026.

The population expansion came through Stelo. In June 2026 the FDA cleared the Stelo glucose biosensor system for children, making it the first over-the-counter CGM cleared for paediatric prediabetic and diabetic patients. Over-the-counter access removes the prescription gate entirely, and paediatric clearance extends it to a population that was previously unreachable without a physician.

Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was raised slightly to $5.18-5.25 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin around 64%, operating margin of 23.5-24% and adjusted EBITDA margin of 31.5-32%.

Risks are competitive and reimbursement-driven: Abbott's FreeStyle Libre franchise competing directly, Medicare durable medical equipment reimbursement pressure, and the long-run question of whether GLP-1 adoption reduces diabetes prevalence.

entries.name: TAVR Sapien & Transcatheter Mitral/Tricuspid
entries.thesisShort: Edwards leads structural heart with Sapien TAVR, and its transcatheter mitral and tricuspid business grew 47% in Q2 2026 to $195.9 million with full-year guidance raised to $760-780 million.
entries.thesisLong:
Edwards Lifesciences built the transcatheter aortic valve replacement market and is now building the mitral and tricuspid one, which is the larger and less penetrated opportunity.

Q2 2026 sales were $1.74 billion, up 12.5%, with adjusted EPS of $0.78. TAVR contributed $1.3 billion, up 10.5%, supported by sustained clinical momentum and a competitor's prior-year exit, with Sapien holding its position as the durability benchmark. TMTT — the Pascal and Evoque platforms addressing mitral and tricuspid disease — grew 47.3% to $195.9 million, or 44.8% in constant currency.

Management raised guidance across the board: full-year sales growth to 10-11% from 9-11%, TAVR growth to 8-9% from 7-9%, and TMTT to $760-780 million from $740-780 million, implying total company sales of $6.6-6.9 billion and TAVR sales of $4.75-5.0 billion. Adjusted EPS guidance of $2.95-3.05 was reaffirmed even while assuming the effective tax rate lands at the high end of the original 16-19% range — a raise on revenue absorbed without an EPS cut.

The long-run framing management has set is TMTT reaching $2 billion of revenue by 2030, supported by Pascal for tricuspid and next-generation Capture Clarity technology. Getting from under $800 million to $2 billion in four years is roughly a 27% compound rate in a category where procedure adoption depends on training centres and reimbursement, not just device availability.

Risks are competitive and regulatory: Medtronic and Abbott competing across both TAVR and transcatheter repair, and reimbursement tightening on novel structural heart procedures.

entries.name: da Vinci Robotic Surgery Platform
entries.thesisShort: Intuitive's da Vinci installed base reached 11,710 systems at 30 June 2026, up 12% year over year, with worldwide procedures growing 16% and revenue up 19% to $2.89 billion.
entries.thesisLong:
Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci is the global standard for soft-tissue robotic surgery, and the business compounds through a razor-and-blade structure: systems are placed, then generate instrument and accessory revenue on every procedure performed for the life of the system.

Both halves grew in Q2 2026. The installed base reached 11,710 systems as of 30 June 2026, up 12% from 10,488 a year earlier, on 468 placements in the quarter against 395 in Q2 2025 — of which 246 were da Vinci 5 systems, up from 180. Worldwide procedures across da Vinci and Ion grew approximately 16%, with da Vinci procedures up 15% and Ion procedures up 36%. Revenue was $2.89 billion, up 19% from $2.44 billion.

The combination is what makes this a bottleneck rather than a growth story. Procedure growth running ahead of installed base growth means utilisation per system is rising, so the recurring revenue base compounds faster than the capital placements that create it. And every additional year of surgeon training on da Vinci raises the switching cost for the hospitals that would have to retrain to move.

Ion's 36% procedure growth is the newer vector — robotic bronchoscopy for lung biopsy addresses a different specialty and a different referral pathway than the surgical franchise.

Competition is now real rather than theoretical: Medtronic's Hugo is establishing international positions and Johnson & Johnson's Ottava is entering clinical use. Component tariffs are the other operational exposure.

entries.name: Mako Orthopedic Robotics
entries.thesisShort: Stryker delivered its best-ever second quarter for Mako installations in both US and international markets, with 9% organic sales growth to roughly $6.3 billion and adjusted EPS up 17.9%.
entries.thesisLong:
Stryker's Mako platform is the orthopaedic counterpart to da Vinci: place the robot, then pull through the implants and instruments used in every procedure it performs. Once a surgeon plans cases on Mako software and a hospital has standardised on Stryker implants, the switching cost spans both capital and consumables.

Q2 2026 delivered 9% organic sales growth to approximately $6.3 billion with adjusted EPS of $3.69, up 17.9%. The company recorded its best-ever second quarter for Mako installations in both US and international markets, and utilisation across the installed base continued to rise. US Orthopaedics organic sales grew 9.2% driven by those installations, MedSurg and Neurotechnology grew 9.2% organically, and orthopaedics overall grew 8.6%.

Rising utilisation on a growing base is the mechanic that matters. Capital placements are lumpy and hospital budget-dependent; the implant and instrument pull-through they create is recurring, and it compounds with every additional procedure performed on each installed system.

Stryker narrowed full-year 2026 guidance to organic sales growth of 8.3-9.3%, from 8-9.5%, and adjusted EPS of $14.95-15.10, citing strong orders, production ramp and stable procedural trends — and resumed share repurchases. The quarter was delivered while recovering from a cyber incident and associated one-time charges, which makes the underlying operating performance somewhat better than the headline.

Competition from Johnson & Johnson's Velys and Zimmer Biomet's Rosa continues, and ambulatory surgery centre reimbursement shifts affect how capital equipment is purchased.

entries.name: Austedo & Biosimilars Engine
entries.thesisShort: Teva's innovative brands are carrying the company — Austedo, Uzedy and Ajovy grew a combined 43% in Q2 2026 — but total revenue slipped 1% to about $4.1 billion with a GAAP net loss of $576 million.
entries.thesisLong:
Teva's pivot from a generics business into a branded-plus-biosimilars business is visible in the composition of its results and, so far, not in the total.

Q2 2026 revenue was approximately $4.1 billion, down 1% year over year, with a GAAP net loss of $576 million, or $0.49 per share. Underneath that, the three innovative brands grew a combined 43%: Austedo up 40%, Uzedy up 43% and Ajovy up 56%. Teva raised its full-year revenue outlook for all three. The divergence between a 43% growth engine and a flat consolidated top line is the whole story — the branded portfolio is compounding fast but is not yet large enough to offset generics pricing pressure across the rest of the business.

Biosimilars are the second leg and are running ahead of plan. Teva now expects to exceed its target of $800 million in biosimilar revenue by 2027, with 15 biosimilars already in market and 14 more in the pipeline. Biosimilars sit in a genuinely defensible position for a company with Teva's manufacturing base: they require regulatory and production capability that pure generics competitors lack, but do not carry the discovery risk of novel drugs.

The risk is arithmetic. Until the innovative and biosimilar portfolios are large enough to outweigh the declining base, consolidated growth stays near zero regardless of how fast the growth products compound — and drug pricing reform pressure applies to both halves.

Biosimilar revenue expected to exceed the $800M 2027 target
14 additional biosimilars in the pipeline
Uzedy and Ajovy each growing above 40%
risks: Consolidated revenue still declining despite 43% growth in the innovative portfolio
GAAP net loss of $576M in the quarter
US generics pricing pressure persisting
Drug pricing reform compressing biosimilar economics

entries.name: Direct-to-Consumer Telehealth Platform
entries.thesisShort: Hims & Hers has completed its pivot from compounded GLP-1s into branded distribution, growing Q2 2026 revenue 38% to $753.2 million under a March 2026 Novo Nordisk agreement to sell injectable and oral Wegovy and Ozempic.
entries.thesisLong:
Hims & Hers spent 2025 as a compounded-GLP-1 seller and 2026 as a branded distribution partner, and the transition has gone considerably better than the risk framing implied.

On 9 March 2026, Novo Nordisk and Hims & Hers announced an agreement to sell branded GLP-1 medications — including injectable and oral forms of Wegovy and Ozempic — through the Hims & Hers telehealth platform. Novo has since described Hims as one of its most voluminous telehealth partners. The timing was fortunate: the launch of Novo's Wegovy pill removed both the needle objection and part of the price objection for consumers, and Hims was positioned as a primary channel for it.

Q2 2026 revenue was $753.2 million, up 38.2% year over year, with adjusted EBITDA of $60.3 million and international revenue of $131 million. The company raised its full-year forecast to $3.3 billion. International expansion is following the same product: Germany and the UK generated tens of thousands of waitlist sign-ups within days of preparing for the Wegovy pill launch.

The structural question this entry exists to track is whether a distribution platform captures durable economics or is disintermediated. Hims does not own the molecule; it owns the customer relationship, the prescribing workflow and the subscription. Manufacturers running their own direct channels are the standing competitive threat, and platform economics depend on customer acquisition cost staying below lifetime value across the non-GLP-1 verticals too.

entries.name: Plasma-Derived Immunoglobulins
entries.thesisShort: Grifols' immunoglobulin franchise grew 12.8% at constant currency in the first half of 2026, led by 17.7% subcutaneous growth, while first-half net profit rose 28.7% to EUR 227 million.
entries.thesisLong:
Plasma is a genuine physical bottleneck: immunoglobulin cannot be synthesised, so every gram traces back to a donor, a collection centre and a fractionation plant with multi-year lead times. Grifols owns one of the three global collection and fractionation networks.

First-half 2026 net revenue was EUR 3.574 billion, up 2.6% at constant currency, with Q2 net revenue of EUR 1.874 billion. Net profit through June rose 28.7% to EUR 227 million, and cash flow improved materially on refinancing. Management held full-year guidance.

Immunoglobulins are doing the work. The franchise grew 12.8% at constant currency in the first half — intravenous IG up 12.5% on Gamunex demand in the US and Europe, and subcutaneous IG up 17.7%, driven by strong second-quarter commercial growth in Xembify. Subcutaneous administration lets patients dose at home rather than in an infusion centre, which is why it grows faster than the intravenous format and why it expands the treated population rather than merely shifting it.

The most strategically important disclosure concerns supply geography. Grifols expects ex-US plasma collections to increase roughly 2.5 times by 2029, with Egypt accounting for around half, reducing reliance on US-sourced plasma for international markets. Plasma supply has been overwhelmingly American for decades because of compensated donation rules; diversifying the collection base is the structural fix to a single-country dependency.

For the second half, Grifols projects mid-to-high single-digit IG growth in core markets, continued strong double-digit subcutaneous growth, and stabilising albumin comparisons as China pricing normalisation completes.

Risks include FcRn antagonists displacing IG in some autoimmune indications, China albumin pricing, and donor compensation regulation.

entries.name: Companion Animal Pharmaceuticals
entries.thesisShort: Zoetis remains the global animal health leader, but Q2 2026 revenue was flat at $2.5 billion with US sales down 7%, and management cut full-year guidance to $9.12-9.32 billion from $9.68-9.96 billion.
entries.thesisLong:
Zoetis is the global animal health leader, and 2026 has been the year the US companion animal business stopped compounding.

Q2 2026 revenue was $2.5 billion, flat against the prior year and down 1% on an organic operational basis. The US segment fell to $1.3 billion, down 7% both reported and organically. Management cut full-year 2026 guidance to revenue of $9.12-9.32 billion and adjusted diluted EPS of $6.15-6.25, from a prior $9.68-9.96 billion, implying organic operational growth of negative 3% to negative 1% for the year. A guidance cut of that magnitude mid-year is the most important fact in this entry and reverses the recovery framing that previously applied.

The osteoarthritis pain franchise is the specific problem. Canine OA pain monoclonal antibodies — Librela and Lenivia combined — delivered $105 million, down 8%, with the US portion at $51 million, down 18% and canine OA mAbs specifically down 24%. Management attributed the decline to a high year-over-year comparison, softer clinic visit trends, and a value-conscious consumer environment affecting premium therapies generally.

That last point is the one worth separating out. If the driver is pet-owner spending restraint rather than product-specific safety perception, then the weakness extends beyond one franchise and is a demand condition rather than a marketing problem — which is consistent with the full-year cut rather than a product-level reset.

International and livestock businesses continued to grow but were not large enough to offset the US decline.
catalysts: International and livestock businesses continuing to grow
Lenivia broadening the canine OA pain portfolio alongside Librela
Companion animal dermatology franchise
Comparison base easing after a high prior-year quarter
risks: Full-year guidance cut with organic growth now guided negative
US segment revenue down 7% year over year
Value-conscious pet-owner spending affecting premium therapies broadly
Softer veterinary clinic visit trends

entries.name: Acute Care Hospital Network
entries.thesisShort: HCA grew Q2 2026 revenue 8.7% to $20.23 billion on 2.5% same-facility admissions growth, but now expects health insurance exchange payer-mix losses of $1.0-1.2 billion for the year, up from $600-900 million.
entries.thesisLong:
HCA is the largest US for-profit hospital operator, and its scale advantage runs through commercial payer negotiations, trauma and tertiary referral capture, and an ambulatory network that keeps patients inside the system.

Q2 2026 volumes were solid where it counts. Revenue rose 8.7% to $20.230 billion, net income was $1.699 billion, up 2.8%, and diluted EPS was $7.62, up 11.6%, on adjusted EBITDA of $4.027 billion. Same-facility admissions grew 2.5%, equivalent admissions 2.7% and emergency room visits 3.6% — though inpatient surgeries fell 2.3% and outpatient surgeries 3.4%.

The defining issue is payer mix rather than volume. Reduced Affordable Care Act exchange enrolment shifted patients into uninsured status — HCA has described the exchange volume dropoff as almost one-for-one converting to uninsurance — which reduced income before income taxes by roughly $400 million in the quarter alone. HCA had guided in April to a $600-900 million full-year unfavourable impact; it now expects $1.0-1.2 billion. That escalation is the single most important change in this entry, and it is a policy outcome rather than an operating one.

Offsetting it, approximately $400 million of incremental net benefit came from Medicaid Supplemental Payment Programs, largely a Florida directed payment programme that added $1.372 billion of revenue and $829 million of other operating expense for periods back to 1 October 2024.

Updated 2026 guidance is revenue of $39.5-40.5 billion and EPS of $15.20-16.10. The risks are all policy-shaped: further coverage erosion, site-of-service payment parity, 340B restrictions, and labour cost re-acceleration.
